title: K-th Largest Value
fine: Heap: top k and k-way merge
statement:
A monitoring service collects request latencies in milliseconds. To set an alert threshold it needs the k-th slowest request of the batch: the k-th largest value. The batch is large and k is small, so you want to keep only the k values that matter instead of ordering all of them.

Write def solution(nums, k) that returns the k-th largest value in nums, counting duplicates: it is the value at position k (1-based) if you sorted nums from largest to smallest. In [5, 5, 4] the 1st and 2nd largest are both 5 and the 3rd is 4. Do not modify the caller's list. Aim for O(n log k) time with a heap of size k.

examples.why: From largest: 6, 5, ... so the 2nd largest is 5.
From largest: 6, 5, 5, 4. Both 5s take a place.
Duplicates count, so the 2nd largest of two equal values is that value.

think.q: Do duplicates count as separate places?
think.a: Yes. The answer is a position in the sorted order, not the k-th distinct value. In [3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6] sorted from largest: 6, 5, 5, 4, ... so the 4th largest is 4, and both 5s take a place.

think.q: Keep the 2 largest values of [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4] as you read left to right. Which one is the answer?
think.a: Read 3: {3}. Read 2: {2, 3}. Read 1: smaller than both, skip. Read 5: drop 2, {3, 5}. Read 6: drop 3, {5, 6}. Read 4: smaller than 5, skip. The 2 largest are {5, 6}, and the answer is the smaller of them, 5. At each step you only compared with the smallest kept value.

think.q: What is the first idea that works?
think.a: Sort and index: sorted(nums)[-k], O(n log n). Slower still: remove the maximum k times, O(n * k). Both work; the heap keeps the memory at O(k) and the time at O(n log k), which matters when the data is a stream.

A min-heap of size k. The heap holds the k largest values seen so far, and its root heap[0] is the smallest of them: the current k-th largest. A new value only matters if it beats the root; then it replaces the root. Python's heapq is a min-heap, which is exactly what you need here.

1. heap = [].
  2. For each value: if the heap has fewer than k items, heappush it.
  3. Otherwise, if the value is greater than heap[0], heapreplace(heap, value) (pop the root and push the value in one step).
  4. Return heap[0].

k = 1 (the maximum) and k = len(nums) (the minimum). All values equal. Negative values and zeros. Duplicates around the k-th place. A value equal to the root: replacing it changes nothing, so > and >= both give the right answer.

hints: You only need the k largest values, not a full sort. Which of those k is the answer?
Keep the k largest values in a min-heap. Its smallest item, heap[0], is the k-th largest so far.
Push until the heap has k items. After that, a value only enters if it is greater than heap[0]: use heapq.heapreplace(heap, value).
explain:
Example 2, nums = [3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6], k = 4:

  • Push 3, 2, 3, 1. The heap holds {1, 2, 3, 3}; its root is 1.
  • 2 > 1: replace, heap {2, 2, 3, 3}. 4 > 2: replace, {2, 3, 3, 4}. 5 > 2: replace, {3, 3, 4, 5}.
  • 5 > 3: replace, {3, 4, 5, 5}. 6 > 3: replace, {4, 5, 5, 6}.
  • The root is 4.

The heap always holds the 4 largest values read so far. Any value that is not greater than the root cannot be in the final top 4, because 4 larger-or-equal values already exist. Each push or replace costs O(log k), so the total is O(n log k) time and O(k) memory. heapq.nlargest(k, nums)[-1] does the same in one line. A quickselect (partition like quicksort, recurse into one side) gets O(n) on average.
complexity: O(n log k) time, O(k) extra space
